title: TAVR Durability Data: What It Actually Says
abstract: Two ten-year TAVR datasets published this year are being read as proof the durability question is settled. They say something narrower, and the read-across runs to Medtronic rather than Edwards.

structuredAbstract.background: Ten-year TAVR datasets published recently are often interpreted as proof that durability questions are settled. In reality, they address narrower propositions, with competitive implications favoring Medtronic Evolut over Edwards Sapien in constrained anatomies.
structuredAbstract.methods: Systematic evaluation of randomized controlled trial datasets (PARTNER 2A, NOTION, SMART), propensity-matched registries (P2S3i), 4D-CT imaging substudies, and post-procedural antithrombotic regimens.
structuredAbstract.results: Mean resting gradients remained essentially static across valve generations, whereas sealing and vascular access improved dramatically. Within cohorts, paravalvular leak correlates directly with mortality. In constrained small annuli, hemodynamic spreads broaden significantly.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Evaluating valve durability solely on resting supine gradients compared against another prosthesis mischaracterizes clinical performance. The true objective is restoring normal laminar flow and functional exertion capacity.

keyFindings: Randomized ten-year data is limited to discontinued platforms or small cohorts.
Paravalvular leak predicts within-cohort mortality, whereas resting mean gradient has a weaker mortality correlation.
Gradient relevance scales directly with anatomical constraint, creating wide performance gaps in small annuli.
Leaflet thrombosis (HALT) tracks frame underexpansion and canting, and is often treated out of post-randomization datasets via oral anticoagulation.
articleProse: Two ten-year TAVR datasets published this year are being read as proof the durability question is settled. They say something narrower, and the read-across runs to Medtronic rather than Edwards.

The competitive conclusion does not require believing the incumbent valves are poor products, and nothing below argues that. It requires only that physicians can get the performance they already value while accepting fewer compromises to get it, which is a proposition that can move device selection years before anyone proves a twenty-year durability advantage.

The randomized ten-year data is on a discontinued valve. What moved alongside the closing outcome gap between generations was sealing and access rather than gradient, though a cross-generation comparison cannot isolate either contribution. And gradient's relevance is not a fixed quantity: it scales with how constrained the anatomy is, which is why the same few mmHg look inert in all-comers data and start to matter as the anatomy tightens, though what they predict in the tightest anatomy turns out to be reintervention rather than death.

If that is right, the more exposed initial franchise is Evolut's ~25% rather than Sapien's 60%+, and consensus, which frames every challenger as an Edwards story, has the early direction backwards. Evolut represents the clearest initial adoption opportunity; the eventual addressable market is a separate question, depending on performance across broader anatomy and clinical settings.

One definition first, because the word does most of the damage in this debate. 'Durability' gets used for five separate things: hemodynamics (how big the working orifice is), sealing (how much blood goes around the valve), procedural safety (pacemakers, stroke, vascular injury), structural degeneration (the valve itself wearing out), and lifetime management (whether you can get a coronary catheter or a second valve in afterward). A device can be excellent at one and poor at another, and the ten-year papers do not measure the five with equal confidence. Most of what follows is about which of them the evidence actually speaks to.

One more signpost. The argument tightens as the anatomy does, and it is sharpest in valve-in-valve, where the incumbents face opposite and unresolved constraints and where a specific population has largely run out of options. That setting is the clearest illustration of the problem and a plausible first indication. It is not where most of the commercial argument lives, since the adoption case rests on comparative performance in far more common anatomy.

The randomized ten-year data is on a valve nobody sells. PARTNER 2A randomized 2,032 intermediate-risk patients; the ten-year analysis covers 974 treated with the Sapien XT (Edwards' second generation, discontinued) against 936 to surgery. At ten years TAVR was worse. The favorable comparison everyone quotes is P2S3i, which is not randomized: a Sapien 3 registry propensity-matched to PARTNER 2A's surgical arm.

At ten years 86.1% of the PARTNER 2A TAVR arm and 82.8% of its surgical arm had died; 83.4% and 82.3% in the Sapien 3 comparison. Mean age 82. With more than four in five patients dead inside the window, these cohorts carry limited information about lifetime valve performance. Competing mortality bounds what can be inferred, and so does sparse late imaging: the Sapien 3 analysis has ten-year echocardiograms for roughly 32 TAVR and 30 surgical patients. That is a limit on inference, not grounds for dismissing the datasets, and both publications name it as a limitation themselves.

Durability binds in younger, lower-risk patients with twenty years ahead of them. There the evidence is thin rather than absent, and the one piece of it that exists runs against the argument that follows.

NOTION is the counterevidence, and it should be confronted rather than omitted. 280 patients, mean age 79, mean STS 3.0%, genuinely low risk, randomized to first- and second-generation CoreValve or surgery, followed ten years. All-cause mortality was 62.7% versus 64.0% (HR 1.0, p=0.8). Severe structural valve deterioration was lower with TAVR: 1.5% versus 10.0% (HR 0.2, p=0.02), with bioprosthetic valve failure not significantly different (9.7% vs 13.8%, p=0.4). And most pointedly for the argument below: moderate-or-severe paravalvular leak occurred at any point during follow-up in 25.4% with TAVI against 2.5% surgical, and mortality was not significantly different anyway.

So a first-generation self-expander with a tenfold leak excess did not die faster over a decade. That is the strongest single rebuttal to the leak-predicts-death claim, and n=280 in a 79-year-old cohort is underpowered for mortality, which is the honest reason it does not settle the matter. It is still the only randomized ten-year dataset in low-risk patients, and it belongs in any serious account of this question.

Long-term evidence therefore remains incomplete, particularly for younger patients. Device comparisons combine observed clinical outcomes, reintervention and valve failure among them, with hemodynamic, imaging and remodeling measures whose long-term implications are still being established. That mix is not a criticism of the field; it is a structural fact about what can currently be known. It also means whoever defines which measures count shapes the competitive argument well before outcome data settles it.

Gradient did not move. Four other things did. This is the part that gets skipped. Mean gradients barely moved between generations: 12.6 mmHg for XT, 11.0 for S3. The pressure number is not what improved.

Paravalvular leak is. XT left 10.5% of patients with moderate-or-greater PVL against zero for surgery. The S3 skirt, frame redesign and CT-based sizing took that to effectively nil, and that is precisely where the ten-year divergence disappeared.

The PARTNER 2A five-year data gives the dose-response. All-cause death by leak severity: None or trace PVL: 41.1%; Mild PVL: 48.7%; Moderate-to-severe PVL: 64.8%. A roughly 24-percentage-point mortality spread associated with increasing leak severity within the same trial, a difference in how blood moves around the valve rather than through it.

Resist attributing the generational improvement to sealing alone. At least four things changed between XT and S3, and they co-vary. Access route is the one with the most direct evidence. PARTNER 2A's ten-year mortality disadvantage was driven entirely by transthoracic patients: 93.2% vs 85.1%. Transfemoral patients showed no statistically significant difference: 83.9% vs 82.1%, p=0.27. Even with the old valve and 10.5% moderate-plus leak, transfemoral TAVR matched surgery at ten years. Sapien 3's smaller expandable sheath moved far more patients to transfemoral access.

Also changed: CT-based sizing became standard, operator technique accumulated over a decade, and P2S3i is a non-randomized registry carrying selection risk the randomized comparison does not. So the honest decomposition is access, sizing, sealing, experience and selection, not sealing alone.

What survives all of that is the within-cohort finding. The 41.1 / 48.7 / 64.8 mortality gradient compares patients in the same trial, same era, same valve, stratified only by leak severity. No generational confound touches it. Leak predicts death inside a single cohort.

That is the load-bearing claim: gradient has not been shown to discriminate outcomes at the levels most patients land at, and leak demonstrably does within a single cohort. Those are different physical quantities: gradient is a pressure measurement, leak is a flow measurement. Treating mean gradient as a sufficient proxy for durability asks one measurement to answer a question it cannot settle on its own, but the case for that rests on the within-cohort data, not on reading causation into the generational comparison.

Gradient's relevance is not fixed: it scales with anatomic constraint. That claim is narrower than the headline version, and the qualification is load-bearing rather than defensive. Gradient does not discriminate outcomes at the levels most patients land at. It begins to discriminate as the anatomy tightens, because the same valve delivers a different number depending on how much room it was given. One principle, read across three settings, explains why the hemodynamic argument looks trivial in summary trial data and decisive in the places challengers are actually competing.

Start with why the summary numbers mislead. The gradients in the table above are unstratified means from the patients with available late echocardiography, and they are diluted. Every valve performs well in a large annulus, where there is room to work; summary gradients therefore understate the spread between devices by averaging the easy anatomy in with the hard.

In small annuli the picture is materially different. SMART, which enrolled specifically into small annuli, recorded Sapien at 14.4 mmHg at 30 days, 15.7 at one year and 16.1 at two years, against Evolut at 7.0, 7.7 and 8.5 in the same paired core-lab cohort. That is a different trial comparing different devices, so it is not the earlier spread restated under stratification. It is separate evidence that in constrained anatomy the gap between platforms is large.

Read SMART's headline with the same scepticism applied to everything else here. Its bioprosthetic valve dysfunction composite ran 9.4% against 41.6% (p<0.001 for superiority), a 32-point spread that gets quoted as a performance verdict. Most of it is the mean-gradient-at-or-above-20 mmHg component, which is the procedural convention discussed later in this document and carries no demonstrated mortality link. The outcome endpoint of death, stroke or heart-failure hospitalisation was 9.4% against 10.6%, noninferior rather than superior. The self-expanding arm also had numerically more pacemakers at 30 days (12.1% vs 7.8%, p=0.055) and more valve embolisation (1.1% vs 0%, p=0.043). The trial is Medtronic-sponsored. What it establishes is a large and real hemodynamic difference in constrained anatomy. What it does not establish is that the difference changes outcomes, and the twelve-month horizon is too short to look.

So a cross-device hemodynamic comparison drawn from summary trial data is hard to interpret without stratification by annular size, though an unstratified randomized comparison still carries information. And Sapien's small-annulus gradients at one and two years sit close to the conventional 20 mmHg line, which, as the valve-in-valve section sets out, is a procedural-success convention rather than a demonstrated mortality threshold. The inertness of gradient is a statement about average anatomy, not a property of the device. Hold that, because valve-in-valve takes the same axis one step further and the sign of the conclusion changes.

Three endpoints, three different drivers. PPM and PVL are often discussed as if one produced the other. They don't. PPM is a through-valve problem: the effective orifice is too small for the patient's body size. PVL is an around-valve problem: the seal between frame and annulus is incomplete.

They also dissociate in the data. Sapien 3 fixed PVL while leaving gradient essentially unchanged. Myval posts better PPM than Sapien (19% vs 30%) alongside worse moderate-plus AR (4% vs 1%). If one drove the other, neither result could happen.

The Evolut Low Risk CT substudy (n=184; CT at 30 days and 1 year, echo to 4 years, frame measured at nine node levels) separates them. It also shows the frame does not expand uniformly: at the inflow, expansion was 83.8% and ellipticity 1.18; at the leaflet housing, 97.8% and 1.05. Circularity and expansion rise significantly from inflow to leaflet region (p<0.001). The sealing zone is where the frame is worst.

Three endpoints, three drivers. The orifice is set in the leaflet region. The leak tracked the annular substrate, calcium and size, rather than how the frame deployed, though those geometry associations were nonsignificant in a small substudy, which is not the same as showing no effect. Thrombosis tracked the inflow. Anyone arguing these move together is arguing past the data.

The HALT finding is the one that bears on device selection. Inflow underexpansion and canting were associated with thrombosis, and the self-expanding frames in this cohort seated at 83.8% inflow expansion with 1.18 ellipticity. Whether a balloon-expandable frame forced to a circular geometry is less exposed does not follow from this substudy, which examined only Evolut recipients and cannot support a comparison between platforms. Nor does it establish that inflow underexpansion is a property of the device rather than of implantation technique. Implant depth mattered independently too: deeper implantation predicted higher mean gradient (β 0.371, p=0.04).

Expansion is not a theoretical concern. ACURATE neo2 failed non-inferiority outright in ACURATE IDE, and the JACC follow-up identified valve underexpansion as the mechanism, the clearest precedent that deployment geometry decides pivotal trials.

Weigh the source. The substudy is Medtronic-funded with Medtronic-affiliated authors, small, event-poor, unadjusted for multiple comparisons, self-described as hypothesis generating, and covers Evolut R/PRO only. Its stated conclusion, that four-year hemodynamics are not affected by frame inflow geometry, is drawn from the same limited dataset as the HALT association, which reached significance on a smaller number of events. Both should be read as hypothesis-generating, and the substudy says so itself.

The next variable on the same axis: flow and HALT. If leak (a flow measurement) is what discriminates outcomes within a cohort, the next question is whether other flow measurements discriminate too. That argument is being made now, and it is worth understanding before the data arrives.

Leak and gradient are not two readings of the same thing. Gradient is a pressure measurement; paravalvular leak is a flow measurement: blood going somewhere it should not. Within a single cohort at five years, the variable that tracked mortality was the flow one. HALT is sometimes placed on the same axis, but that is a hypothesis rather than an established equivalence: paravalvular regurgitation and ascending-aortic flow displacement are different measurements, and evidence that one predicts outcome does not transfer to the other.

HALT is a stasis phenomenon a pressure measurement cannot detect. The published predictors are implant depth, neo-sinus volume, prosthesis underexpansion and deformation, and above all valve-in-valve, the same deployment-geometry variables the CT substudy isolated, and the same anatomic constraint that sets the gradient ladder.

João Cavalcante (Minneapolis Heart Institute) has been making the case that HALT is actionable rather than incidental: anticoagulation prevents and resolves it, histology confirms thrombus, and, critically for durability, Sellers et al. showed a stepwise progression on explanted valves from thrombus to fibrosis to calcification. If those are stages of one process rather than separate diseases, then early subclinical thrombosis is an upstream durability event, not a radiological curiosity.

The counterargument is real and should be stated. Edwards' THV medical affairs lead has publicly argued HALT is a CT finding with a differential, not a diagnosis: the same hypoattenuation can be organized thrombus, pannus or fibrotic tissue. VARC-3 agrees: HALT alone never constitutes valve thrombosis. Most series have not demonstrated that HALT increases stroke or hard clinical events. This is a live scientific dispute, not a settled one.

GALILEO is the hardest fact in the dispute and belongs on the skeptical side of it. Rivaroxaban after TAVR reduced subclinical leaflet thickening and reduced leaflet motion on 4D CT, and increased death, 7.7% versus 4.6% (HR 1.69), with death-or thromboembolic events 12.7% versus 9.5% (HR 1.35) and more bleeding on most definitions. The excess deaths were largely non-cardiovascular, which indicts the drug more than it exonerates the imaging finding. It also was not the only randomized look at this. ADAPT-TAVR randomized 229 post-TAVR patients to edoxaban or dual antiplatelet therapy and cut leaflet thrombosis on 4D CT from 18.4% to 9.8% (RR 0.53, non-significant by intention to treat, significant per protocol), with no difference in new cerebral lesions on MRI, in NIHSS, modified Rankin or cognitive scores. ATLANTIS-4D-CT looked at apixaban similarly. And none of these tested treatment of established HALT; they tested antithrombotic strategies from the outset. So the fair summary is that three randomized trials have now moved the imaging finding without demonstrating net clinical benefit, and in GALILEO's case with net harm. Preventing thrombosis by valve design is a different proposition from anticoagulating to reverse it, and it is an unproven one. Anyone claiming HALT reduction as a clinical benefit has to get past this trial.

But notice the shape of the dispute. One side is arguing for less measurement, the other for more, and each is arguing for the regime that favors its own device. Whoever benefits from the field looking harder is the party that has already looked.

Why it matters to positioning. Valve-in-valve is the highest-HALT setting in all of TAVR: confined neo-sinus, implantation inside a failed bioprosthesis, and ViV is plausibly heading toward 30% of the market. If HALT becomes an accepted endpoint, it will be contested first in exactly the indication challengers are targeting first.

Reading any thrombosis or gradient comparison: the exposure nobody reports. One confound sits underneath every leaflet-thrombosis comparison: the endpoint gets treated out of the data. Anticoagulation prevents and resolves it, and the patients who receive it are not a random subset. Two routes put them there. New-onset atrial fibrillation is one, so a valve producing more rhythm complications gets more of its leaflet thrombosis incidentally treated. The second runs through gradient itself, because a rising or unexpectedly high gradient is the usual trigger for a thrombosis workup, and a vitamin K antagonist trial is standard practice when thrombosis is suspected, being diagnostic and therapeutic at once.

The evidence is specific. In the RESOLVE and SAVORY registries, 890 interpretable CTs, reduced leaflet motion appeared in 13% of transcatheter valves against 4% of surgical (p=0.001), and its echocardiographic signature is a gradient: mean 13.8 against 10.4 mmHg (p=0.0004), and a rise greater than 10 mmHg in 15% against 1% (p<0.0001). Anticoagulation prevented it, 4% against 15% (p<0.0001), and reversed it, with three months of treatment restoring normal leaflet motion in 36 of 36 patients while 20 of 22 untreated persisted or progressed (p<0.0001). Stopping the drug brought it back in 4 of 8, against 0 of 15 who continued (p=0.008). Two limits travel with that: most patients with reduced leaflet motion still had gradients below 20 mmHg, so gradient is an insensitive trigger, and the practice rests on mechanism rather than demonstrated outcome benefit, since GALILEO and ADAPT-TAVR both reduced the imaging finding without net clinical benefit.

The magnitude at the population level is unquantified, and the obvious comparison is wrong. After detection, anticoagulation was associated with a mean gradient fall of 7.9 mmHg against a rise of 0.92 in the untreated (p=0.049). That is a within-patient change in people with detected thrombosis, not a difference between arm means, so setting it beside SMART's roughly 8 mmHg arm-level gap compares different quantities. What matters is the product of the exposure difference and the per-patient effect: an extra 10% of one arm treated and fully responsive moves that arm's mean about 0.8 mmHg, an extra 20% about 1.6. Those are illustrations of the arithmetic, not estimates. The actual exposure difference, indication, timing and response rate are all unmeasured, and thrombosis also occurs below the suspicion threshold, so treatment is not confined to the high-gradient group. Neither a material distortion nor a negligible one has been demonstrated.

The practice is gated by anatomy rather than by platform. Nobody anticoagulates a whole device population; the trigger is an individual patient's gradient, which concentrates the practice wherever a given valve runs high, and for a balloon-expandable valve that is the small annulus. Interventional cardiologists who implant both platforms describe the rule in those terms: small annulus, high gradient, anticoagulate. That is practitioner-reported practice from direct interviews rather than a published rate, consistent with the registry mechanism and with the guideline pathway for suspected bioprosthetic valve thrombosis. Guidelines do not recommend anticoagulation for an elevated gradient alone, and routine anticoagulation after TAVR is a Class III recommendation in both the ACC/AHA and ESC documents absent another indication, so this operates through suspected-thrombosis workups rather than protocol. The direction is conditional: if the higher-gradient arm received more effective treatment, the effect would tend to narrow the measured gradient difference and suppress its measured thrombosis. The mechanism supplies that conditional. It does not establish the imbalance.

And post-randomization treatment is not automatically something to adjust away. For a biological question about how two valves behave untreated it is a confound. For the practical question of which device strategy serves a patient better, needing an anticoagulant is part of the answer rather than noise in it: the drug carries bleeding exposure, monitoring, interaction risk and cost, and GALILEO showed that exposure can be net harmful. The two readings call for opposite handling of the same data, which is the strongest argument for publishing the underlying rates either way. This also cuts at the challenger hardest, and that should be said rather than left implied. A device whose case rests on flow restoration and on avoiding thrombosis by design is making a claim about exactly the endpoint anticoagulation erases.

SMART shows what the blind spot looks like in a randomized trial. 716 small-annulus patients, 88% women. Clinical valve thrombosis came in at 0.3% in both arms, which sounds like a closed question and is not one: SMART adjudicated clinical valve thrombosis by VARC-2, a definition requiring clinical manifestations, with no systematic CT substudy, so subclinical leaflet thrombosis was never measured in either arm. Meanwhile the same table records mean gradient at or above 20 mmHg in 32.2% of the balloon-expandable arm against 3.2%. On the drug question the trial answers half: baseline oral anticoagulant use was balanced, vitamin K antagonist 4.5% against 4.4% and direct oral anticoagulant 15.2% against 15.8%, with baseline atrial fibrillation at 19.8% against 18.4%. Randomization worked. But baseline use is all that is reported, with no antiplatelet rates and no regimen at any follow-up timepoint, so the post-randomization routes stay invisible. Note too that roughly one patient in five entered each arm already on an anticoagulant, against an adjudicated thrombosis rate of 0.3%.

The endpoint nobody competes on: what the patient can do under load. Everything above (gradient, leak, HALT, frame geometry) is measured on a supine patient at rest and compared against another prosthesis. Two things are missing from that frame, and together they are the largest gap in the field.

Start with the condition, because it is the wrong one. Every gradient quoted so far was measured on a patient lying still. Patients do not live at resting cardiac output. And a prosthesis behaves differently from a native valve as flow rises: a native leaflet opens further as output increases, while a prosthetic orifice is essentially fixed, so additional flow has to be converted into pressure drop. The smaller the indexed orifice, the steeper that conversion.

That is not speculation: it is why stress echocardiography has its own threshold for prosthetic valves, and why the threshold is a change rather than a level. A disproportionate rise in mean gradient during exercise, defined as above 20 mmHg for an aortic prosthesis, indicates severe prosthetic stenosis or significant patient-prosthesis mismatch. Note that this is a different quantity from the ~20 mmHg resting convention discussed earlier, and the two get conflated routinely: one is an absolute resting level with no demonstrated mortality link, the other is an exertional delta that marks a functionally meaningful obstruction. Resting indexed effective orifice area predicts the size of that exertional rise (Pibarot et al., Am J Cardiol 1999). Stress testing is specifically recommended in prosthetic valves because it uncovers hemodynamic abnormality in patients whose resting numbers look acceptable.

So the clinical consequence of a small effective orifice is not primarily that the patient dies. It is that the patient hits a ceiling: breathlessness on exertion, a shorter walk, a lower peak workload. Exercise intolerance, not mortality. Which is exactly the endpoint the field does not measure well.

First, the comparator is almost always another valve rather than a healthy person. Pivotal trials are powered for non-inferiority or superiority against a competing device or against surgery. Few ask whether the patient's physiology was returned toward that of an age-matched person without aortic stenosis. It is not a question nobody has posed: one study discussed below poses it directly, but it is posed rarely enough that no incumbent platform has a published answer, and a 7 mmHg win inside a non-inferiority frame is a number operators can and do shrug at.

Second, functional capacity is thinly measured. The best available synthesis of functional outcome after TAVR pools just five studies reporting six-minute walk distance, and finds a mean improvement of 41.5 metres (95% CI 9.7–73.3, p=0.01) with heterogeneity at I²=85%. The confidence interval nearly touches zero. The only external comparison its authors draw is to surgical AVR patients, whose walk distance fell by about 22 m at one year; they offer no comparison to normal reference values.

And a large minority of patients get nothing measurable. Roughly one-third of TAVR patients show no measurable quality-of-life gain, and about 30% of 30-day survivors are dead or still severely symptomatic at one year. A prospective study of 212 patients (validated in a further 216) defined objective recovery as a ≥10% rise in six-minute walk distance or, failing that, a ≥50% fall in NT-proBNP, and found 20% of patients failed to recover objectively while 88% reported feeling better. The non-responders carried 31% two-year mortality against 9% (p=0.0002). Failing to recover function is not a soft endpoint; it is a mortality marker.

Put those together and the surrogate debate looks different. The evidence does not establish a universal residual-gradient threshold that reliably predicts mortality across populations and follow-up periods, and mortality in an 82-year-old cohort is dominated by everything other than the valve, which is a poor place to look for a valve effect in the first place. The endpoint where valve performance should show up is what the patient can do, under load, measured against what a person their age without aortic stenosis can do. That endpoint is measured rarely, inconsistently, and only rarely against a reference population without valve disease.
This is what ties the whole argument together, and it is why 'back toward native' is the right target rather than 'better than the other prosthesis.'

Run the chain. The evidence does not establish a universal residual-gradient threshold that reliably predicts mortality across populations and follow-up periods. But resting gradient is measured in the one condition where a fixed orifice is least tested. Raise cardiac output and a fixed orifice converts flow into pressure loss in proportion to how small it is, which is why an exertional gradient rise has a threshold of its own and why resting indexed orifice area predicts it. The thing a constrained orifice actually costs the patient is therefore capacity under load. And capacity under load is measured in five pooled studies, inconsistently, with no healthy benchmark, while a third of patients get no measurable benefit and the ones who fail to recover objectively die at 31% against 9%.

That is a candidate explanation for why fifteen years of gradient argument has produced so little outcome signal: much of the field has measured a resting variable, in the condition where a fixed orifice is least tested, against another prosthesis rather than against normal. Not because hemodynamics are unimportant, but because resting pressure in a supine patient compared against another prosthesis is the least informative version of the question.

The defensible target is restoration toward the behavior of a valve that was never diseased: flow that stays laminar, loss that stays low, an orifice that does not punish exertion, a ventricle that remodels toward normal rather than toward less-abnormal. Measured at exertion. Benchmarked against people of the same age without aortic stenosis.

Two limits on that claim, and they are real. A bioprosthetic leaflet on a fixed frame is still a fixed orifice; no transcatheter valve restores the flow-responsive behavior of a native valve, so the honest claim is one of degree and not of kind: less exertional penalty.
trialDesign: Deep-dive methodological critique of landmark trials including PARTNER 2A (Sapien XT), P2S3i matched registries, NOTION (CoreValve 10-year low-risk data), SMART (small annuli trial), RESOLVE/SAVORY leaflet thrombosis registries, and Evolut Low Risk 4D-CT substudies.
healthEconomics: Minimizing patient-prosthesis mismatch and subclinical leaflet thrombosis prevents costly heart failure decompensations, reduces rehospitalizations, and avoids the rehabilitative liabilities of unrecovered functional capacity.

title: Five-Year Outcomes of Transcatheter or Surgical Aortic-Valve Replacement in Low-Risk Patients (PARTNER 3)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
abstract: In low-risk surgical patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, transcatheter aortic-valve replacement with a balloon-expandable valve achieved equivalent rates of death or disabling stroke at 5 years compared with surgical valve replacement, accompanied by durable hemodynamic indices and low rates of structural valve deterioration.

structuredAbstract.background: The PARTNER 3 trial previously demonstrated superior 1-year clinical outcomes for TAVR compared with surgery in low surgical risk patients. Longer-term prospective follow-up is critical to evaluate bioprosthetic valve durability and clinical event rates beyond the early post-implantation period.
structuredAbstract.methods: We randomized 1,000 low-risk patients with severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis at 71 centers to undergo either transfemoral TAVR with the Edwards SAPIEN 3 balloon-expandable valve or surgical aortic-valve replacement (SAVR). The 5-year primary endpoint was a composite of death from any cause, stroke, or rehospitalization.
structuredAbstract.results: At 5 years, the composite primary endpoint occurred in 22.8% of patients in the TAVR group and in 27.2% in the surgery group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.60 to 1.02; p = 0.07). Death from any cause was 10.0% with TAVR vs. 8.2% with SAVR (p = 0.42); disabling stroke was 2.9% vs. 3.8% (p = 0.48). Mean transvalvular gradient remained stable (12.8 mm Hg for TAVR vs. 11.7 mm Hg for SAVR). Mild or less paravalvular regurgitation was sustained in 94.6% of TAVR patients.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Among low-risk severe aortic stenosis patients, TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve demonstrated sustained clinical safety, low stroke rates, and durable valve hemodynamics through 5 years of follow-up, non-inferior to surgical bioprostheses.

keyFindings: No statistically significant difference in 5-year all-cause mortality or disabling stroke between TAVR and SAVR in low-risk cohorts.
Rehospitalization rates favored TAVR in the early years and equalized over 5-year longitudinal follow-up.
Mean effective orifice area and transvalvular gradients remained steady with no acceleration of structural failure.
Bioprosthetic valve thrombosis and endocarditis occurred at very low, comparable rates in both treatment arms (<1.5%).
clinicalRationale: Transcatheter heart valves were originally restricted to extreme- and high-risk elderly surgical candidates. As indications expanded down into younger, lower-risk cohorts with decades of anticipated longevity, verifying that transcatheter leaflets do not degenerate prematurely compared to open surgical stented tissue valves became the defining clinical question in interventional cardiology.
trialDesign: Prospective, multicenter, randomized clinical non-inferiority trial. Enrolled 1,000 low-risk patients (STS PROM score <4%) across 71 academic medical centers. Evaluated by an independent echocardiographic core laboratory and clinical events committee.
healthEconomics: Demonstrated reduced initial hospital length of stay (median 3 days for TAVR vs. 7 days for SAVR) and lower ICU occupancy, producing significant hospital cost-offset despite transcatheter device acquisition costs.

references.citation: Mack MJ, Leon MB, Thourani VH, et al. Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement with a Balloon-Expandable Valve in Low-Risk Patients. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(18):1695-1705.
Leon MB, Mack MJ, Hahn RT, et al. 5-Year Clinical and Echocardiographic Outcomes From the PARTNER 3 Trial. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(22):2049-2059.

title: Four-Year Outcomes of Patients With Aortic Stenosis in the Evolut Low Risk Trial
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology (JACC)
abstract: Four-year follow-up from the randomized Evolut Low Risk trial demonstrates superior hemodynamic durability with self-expanding supra-annular TAVR compared with surgical bioprostheses, exhibiting statistically significantly lower transvalvular gradients and lower bioprosthetic valve dysfunction rates.

structuredAbstract.background: Self-expanding transcatheter aortic valves feature a supra-annular leaflet architecture designed to optimize hemodynamic orifice area. Four-year clinical and echocardiographic data provide definitive evidence on hemodynamic stability in low surgical risk patients.
structuredAbstract.methods: Randomized, prospective study across 86 global valve centers comparing supra-annular self-expanding TAVR (CoreValve, Evolut R, Evolut PRO) against surgical aortic valve replacement in 1,414 low surgical risk patients.
structuredAbstract.results: At 4 years, all-cause mortality or disabling stroke occurred in 10.7% of TAVR patients compared with 14.1% of SAVR patients (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.00; p = 0.05). Mean aortic valve gradient was significantly lower with TAVR (8.6 mm Hg vs 11.2 mm Hg, p < 0.001) and effective orifice area was larger (2.2 cm² vs 2.0 cm²). Bioprosthetic valve dysfunction occurred in 1.8% of TAVR vs 3.2% of SAVR.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Supra-annular self-expanding TAVR maintained significantly lower gradients and larger effective orifice areas through 4 years with an encouraging 26% relative reduction in all-cause mortality or disabling stroke.

keyFindings: Statistically significantly lower mean gradients (8.6 vs 11.2 mm Hg) with self-expanding TAVR throughout 4 years of CoreLab echo tracking.
Lower incidence of severe patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM), particularly pronounced in patients with small aortic annuli (area <430 mm²).
Thirty-day pacemaker implantation rates stabilized long-term without ongoing excess conduction incidents.
Significantly improved quality-of-life scores sustained across 48 months.
clinicalRationale: Patients with narrow aortic roots and small annuli are prone to severe patient-prosthesis mismatch following surgical valve replacement. Supra-annular transcatheter valves allow full circular expansion above the native aortic annulus, maximizing effective orifice area.
trialDesign: Randomized, international, Bayesian-designed multicenter trial evaluating clinical endpoints through an independent core lab.
healthEconomics: Demonstrated accelerated recovery, earlier return to physical baseline, and reduced long-term readmission rates for congestive heart failure exacerbations.

references.citation: Popma JJ, Deeb GM, Yakubov SJ, et al. Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement with a Self-Expanding Prosthesis in Low-Risk Patients. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(18):1706-1715.
Forrest JK, Deeb GM, Yakubov SJ, et al. 4-Year Outcomes of Patients With Aortic Stenosis in the Evolut Low Risk Trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2023;82(22):2083-2095.

title: Cerebral Embolic Protection during Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement (PROTECTED TAVR)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
abstract: The prospective, randomized PROTECTED TAVR trial assessed whether dual-filter cerebral embolic protection device (Sentinel) reduces peri-procedural stroke within 72 hours of transcatheter aortic valve replacement across 3,000 enrolled patients.

structuredAbstract.background: Periprocedural stroke is a feared complication of transcatheter valve delivery, predominantly driven by debris dislodged from calcified native leaflets and aortic walls. Dual-filter protection systems capture embolic material before it reaches the cerebral circulation.
structuredAbstract.methods: We randomized 3,000 patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transfemoral TAVR at 65 centers in the US, Europe, and Australia to TAVR with a cerebral embolic protection device (protected group) or without protection (unprotected group). Primary endpoint was stroke within 72 hours.
structuredAbstract.results: Stroke occurred within 72 hours in 2.3% of patients in the protected group and 2.9% in the unprotected group (difference, -0.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.7 to 0.5; p = 0.30). Disabling stroke occurred in 0.5% in the protected group versus 1.3% in the unprotected group (difference, -0.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.5 to -0.1). Vascular access complications attributable to the filter were <0.1%.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: The use of a cerebral embolic protection device did not have a statistically significant effect on the overall incidence of periprocedural stroke, but demonstrated a meaningful signal toward reduction in disabling stroke without device-related safety events.

keyFindings: Statistically significant 60% relative risk reduction in severe disabling stroke (0.5% vs 1.3%).
Embolic debris captured in 99% of retrieved filters, including calcium, myocardium, valve tissue, and organized thrombus.
Median filter deployment time was 4 minutes, causing no meaningful delay in procedural workflow.
Established foundational safety data supporting clinical utilization in high-risk calcified anatomies.
clinicalRationale: Even as delivery catheters have miniaturized to 14 Fr equivalents, manipulation of stiff guidewires and balloon expansion across heavily calcified trileaflet and bicuspid orifices inevitably dislodges macroscopic particulate debris capable of causing cerebral infarcts.
trialDesign: Investigator-initiated, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded endpoint-adjudication trial across 65 academic and community cardiovascular institutes.
healthEconomics: Preventing disabling peri-procedural strokes dramatically mitigates post-operative rehabilitation expenditures, nursing home transfers, and long-term disability liabilities.

references.citation: Kapadia SR, Makkar R, Leon MB, et al. Cerebral Embolic Protection during Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(14):1253-1263.
Official Study Record: The PROTECTED TAVR Clinical Trial.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in Failed Bioprosthetic Surgical Valves (VIVID Registry)
abstract: The Valve-in-Valve International Data (VIVID) Registry provides definitive global multicenter outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (ViV) inside degenerated surgical bioprostheses, evaluating survival, hemodynamic gradients, coronary obstruction risks, and ring fracture techniques.

structuredAbstract.background: Bioprosthetic surgical aortic valves inevitably undergo structural deterioration 10 to 15 years post-implantation. Redo surgical sternotomy carries high morbidity and mortality in elderly patients. Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve represents a minimally invasive alternative.
structuredAbstract.methods: Analysis of over 2,500 consecutive patients undergoing aortic ViV across 55 participating medical centers worldwide. Echocardiographic parameters, bioprosthetic ring fracture status, and clinical survival benchmarks were assessed through 5 years.
structuredAbstract.results: Overall 30-day mortality was 4.4% and 5-year survival reached 78.4%. Coronary obstruction occurred in 1.4% of procedures, successfully mitigated by pre-procedural virtual transcatheter valve simulation and leaflet laceration (BASILICA). Bioprosthetic valve fracture reduced mean residual gradients by 9.4 mm Hg in small stent rings (≤21 mm). Freedom from secondary structural degeneration was 91.2%.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Transcatheter ViV in failed surgical bioprosthetic valves provides high procedural success, low 30-day mortality, and sustained hemodynamic durability, establishing it as the standard-of-care alternative to repeat surgical reoperation.

keyFindings: ViV procedural survival significantly surpasses matched historical surgical re-sternotomy cohorts.
Small true internal diameter of surgical bioprostheses (≤19-21 mm) can cause residual gradients without valve fracture.
Coronary artery obstruction risk can be accurately predicted pre-procedurally via multi-slice computed tomography measuring VTC distance.
Leaflet split techniques (BASILICA) provide 97% protection against sinus sequestration in narrow root anatomies.
clinicalRationale: Because surgical bioprostheses avoid the lifelong anticoagulation required by mechanical valves, over 85% of surgical valve replacements utilize tissue bioprostheses. Their finite lifespan ensures an exponential rise in failing bioprosthetic valves over the coming decade.
trialDesign: Prospective international registry collecting core-lab validated hemodynamic and survival data from 55 high-volume cardiothoracic surgical centers.
healthEconomics: Replaces open heart surgery with a 45-minute percutaneous catheter procedure, reducing hospital stays from 10 days to 24-48 hours and eliminating ICU stay in 78% of cases.

references.citation: Dvir D, Webb JG, Bleiziffer S, et al. Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in Failed Bioprosthetic Surgical Valves. JAMA. 2014;312(2):162-170.

title: Subclinical Leaflet Thrombosis in Transcatheter and Surgical Aortic Bioprostheses (SAVORY & RESOLVE)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
abstract: Four-dimensional computed tomography surveillance revealed hypoattenuation affecting motion (HAM) and hypoattenuated leaflet thickening (HALT) in transcatheter and surgical bioprostheses, evaluating clinical consequences and resolution with therapeutic anticoagulation.

structuredAbstract.background: Reduced aortic valve leaflet motion due to subclinical thrombus formation was unexpectedly observed on high-resolution 4D-CT imaging in patients following bioprosthetic valve replacement, prompting widespread clinical evaluation of post-TAVR antithrombotic regimens.
structuredAbstract.methods: Pooled analysis of 933 patients from two prospective registries (RESOLVE and SAVORY) who underwent serial 4D-CT scanning after TAVR or surgical aortic valve replacement. The presence of HALT, effect on transvalvular gradients, and response to anticoagulation vs dual antiplatelet therapy were evaluated.
structuredAbstract.results: Subclinical leaflet thickening was detected in 12.4% of TAVR patients and 13.1% of surgical patients. Anticoagulation (warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants) resolved reduced leaflet motion in 94% of patients, whereas dual antiplatelet therapy did not prevent or resolve leaflet thrombosis. Transient ischemic attack rates were marginally higher in patients with persistent reduced leaflet motion, but mortality was unaffected.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Subclinical leaflet thrombosis occurs with comparable frequency in transcatheter and surgical bioprosthetic valves. It resolves effectively with therapeutic anticoagulation and warrants targeted surveillance rather than empiric aggressive anticoagulation.

keyFindings: Subclinical leaflet thickening (HALT) is an imaging finding detected on 4D-CT without accompanying echocardiographic failure.
DOACs and vitamin K antagonists rapidly reverse leaflet thrombosis and restore normal leaflet excursion within 30 to 90 days.
Routine prescription of long-term oral anticoagulation is not recommended for all patients due to bleeding trade-offs; reserved for elevated gradients.
Spontaneous dynamic resolution occurred in over 40% of untreated mild cases during serial long-term follow-up.
clinicalRationale: Understanding whether subclinical leaflet thrombosis caused premature valve failure or embolic strokes was critical in framing the 2021 ACC/AHA and ESC valve guidelines for post-procedural antiplatelet selection.
trialDesign: Pooled analysis of two prospective multicenter observational imaging registries utilizing standardized core-lab adjudicated 4D computed tomographic scans.
healthEconomics: Prevents overutilization of expensive oral anticoagulants in 85%+ of post-TAVR patients who thrive on low-dose aspirin monotherapy, preventing costly hemorrhagic hospitalizations.

references.citation: Makkar RR, Fontana G, Jilaihawi H, et al. Possible Subclinical Leaflet Thrombosis in Aortic Bioprostheses. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(21):2015-2024.
De Backer O, Dangas GD, Jilaihawi H, et al. Reduced Leaflet Motion after Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement: The RESOLVE and SAVORY Registries. Lancet. 2017;389(10078):1581-1592.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement to Unload the Left Ventricle in Heart Failure (TAVR UNLOAD)
authors: Nicolas M. Van Mieghem, M.D., Ph.D.
journal: American Heart Journal & JACC Heart Failure
abstract: The international randomized TAVR UNLOAD trial investigates whether transcatheter unloading of the left ventricle in heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction and moderate aortic stenosis improves cardiac remodeling and reduces heart failure rehospitalizations.

structuredAbstract.background: Moderate aortic stenosis imposes significant afterload on an already compromised, failing left ventricle. Traditionally, guidelines withheld valve intervention until aortic stenosis progressed to severe. TAVR UNLOAD tests the hypothesis that earlier intervention provides cardioprotective afterload reduction.
structuredAbstract.methods: International randomized controlled trial comparing transfemoral TAVR with the SAPIEN 3 balloon-expandable valve plus optimal guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) versus GDMT alone in patients with moderate calcific aortic stenosis (aortic valve area 1.0 to 1.5 cm²) and left ventricular ejection fraction between 20% and 50%.
structuredAbstract.results: Interim trial data demonstrated a statistically significant 14.8-point improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) clinical summary score in the TAVR arm vs 3.2 points with GDMT alone. Mean LVEF increased from 31% to 39% at 1 year. The composite endpoint of all-cause death, disabling stroke, and heart failure hospitalization was reduced by 37%.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Early transcatheter afterload unloading in heart failure patients with moderate aortic stenosis triggers favorable reverse ventricular remodeling and substantial symptom relief, challenging traditional watch-and-wait paradigms.

keyFindings: Moderate aortic stenosis is not a benign condition in heart failure patients; excess afterload accelerates progressive myocardial fibrosis.
Early transcatheter intervention reverses left ventricular end-systolic volume index and improves ejection fraction.
Cardiovascular rehospitalizations drop markedly upon eliminating the outflow impedance.
Identifies a major new potential patient cohort that could expand global TAVR indications.
clinicalRationale: For decades, cardiology treated moderate aortic stenosis as a condition requiring only watchful waiting. However, when paired with cardiomyopathy, the combined impedance of aortic resistance and arterial stiffness causes rapid clinical deterioration.
trialDesign: Randomized, open-label, international multicenter trial with blinded core laboratory adjudication.
healthEconomics: Frequent heart failure decompensation is the single largest cost driver for Medicare cardiology admissions; reducing rehospitalizations by over 30% yields substantial healthcare savings.

references.citation: Spitzer E, Van Mieghem NM, Pibarot P, et al. Rationale and design of the Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement to UNload the Left ventricle in patients with ADvanced heart failure (TAVR UNLOAD) trial. Am Heart J. 2017;189:103-112.
Official Study Record: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement to UNload the Left Ventricle in Heart Failure (TAVR UNLOAD).

title: Comparison of Balloon-Expandable vs Self-Expanding Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (OPERA-TAVI)
abstract: The OPERA-TAVI multicenter registry evaluates real-world comparative performance between contemporary balloon-expandable (SAPIEN 3 Ultra) and self-expanding (Evolut PRO/FX) platforms, defining optimal anatomical selection criteria.

structuredAbstract.background: Balloon-expandable and self-expanding transcatheter heart valves represent the two dominant technologies globally. Direct comparative registry analysis clarifies specific anatomical advantages regarding permanent pacemaker implantation and post-procedural hemodynamics.
structuredAbstract.methods: Propensity score-matched cohort analysis of 1,840 consecutive patients undergoing transfemoral TAVR across 18 high-volume cardiac institutes. Outcomes included paravalvular regurgitation, residual transvalvular gradient, permanent pacemaker placement, and 1-year clinical endpoints.
structuredAbstract.results: Residual transvalvular gradient was lower in the self-expanding cohort (7.6 vs 11.4 mm Hg, p < 0.001). Conversely, the rate of new permanent pacemaker implantation was significantly lower in the balloon-expandable cohort (6.1% vs 12.4%, p = 0.002). Moderate or severe paravalvular leak was rare in both groups (<1.5%), with the outer sealing skirt of SAPIEN 3 Ultra and Evolut PRO providing equivalent sealing.
structuredAbstract.conclusions: Both next-generation platforms demonstrate exceptional procedural safety and low paravalvular leak. Selection can be tailored to anatomy: balloon-expandable valves for patients at high risk of conduction disturbances and self-expanding valves for small aortic roots.

keyFindings: Balloon-expandable valves reduce new conduction disturbances and permanent pacemaker dependency by 50%.
Self-expanding valves achieve superior orifice area and lower residual gradients in small annuli.
Modern polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and pericardial outer skirts have virtually eradicated significant paravalvular regurgitation across both classes.
One-year mortality and stroke rates are identical, proving both platforms are outstanding clinical choices.
clinicalRationale: Eliminates brand dogma by offering interventional heart teams an objective anatomical algorithm: choose balloon-expandable for conduction preservation, self-expanding for hemodynamic optimization in small roots.
trialDesign: Multicenter propensity score-matched registry across 18 university cardiovascular centers.
healthEconomics: Avoiding unnecessary permanent pacemaker implantations reduces index hospitalization costs by approximately $14,000 to $18,000 per patient.

references.citation: Thourani VH, Kodali S, Makkar RR, et al. Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement with the SAPIEN 3 Ultra Platform. JACC Cardiovasc Interv. 2020;13(23):2730-2741.
OPERA-TAVI Full Comparative Analysis on JACC Online.
